public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Written on the Wall II - Conjecture 4

*Reference:*
[E. DeLaVina, Written on the Wall II, Conjectures of Graffiti.pc](http://cms.dt.uh.edu/faculty/delavinae/research/wowII/)
-/

@[expose] public section


namespace WrittenOnTheWallII.GraphConjecture4

open SimpleGraph

variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]

/--
WOWII [Conjecture 4](http://cms.dt.uh.edu/faculty/delavinae/research/wowII/)

If `G` is a connected graph then the maximum number of leaves over all spanning
trees satisfies `Ls(G) ≥ NG(G) - 1` where `NG(G)` is the minimal neighbourhood
size of a non-edge of `G`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem conjecture4 (G : SimpleGraph α) [DecidableRel G.Adj] [Nontrivial α] (h_conn : G.Connected) :
    NG G - 1 ≤ Ls G := by
  sorry

end WrittenOnTheWallII.GraphConjecture4

reformulations.difference: The source's 'minimum of |N_G(ē)|' is a minimum over nonedges and is undefined when G has no nonedge (complete graphs, including K_1). `SimpleGraph.NG` falls back to `Fintype.card α` (= n) when `Gᶜ.edgeFinset` is empty, and the theorem adds `[Nontrivial α]`. So on complete graphs K_n (n ≥ 2) the Lean theorem also claims n - 1 ≤ Ls(K_n), which the source does not state explicitly.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For non-complete connected graphs the Lean statement is the source's inequality verbatim. `Gᶜ.edgeFinset` is exactly the set of 2-element independent sets {u,v}. `non_edge_neighborhood_card` is |N(u) ∪ N(v)|, matching WOWII definition 8 ('the set of vertices adjacent (in G) to at least one of u or v'). `Ls` is the maximum number of degree-1 vertices over spanning trees, matching definition 1. On complete graphs the extra claim Ls(K_n) ≥ n-1 is trivially true: the spanning star has n-1 leaves for n ≥ 3, and K_2 has 2 ≥ 1. I checked the tight case n = 4 in Lean (`NG ⊤ = 4` and `3 ≤ Ls ⊤` on `Fin 4`). The source's own proof begins 'We can assume that G is of diameter more than one', i.e. it treats the complete case as trivial. `[Nontrivial α]` only removes K_1, where the source's expression is undefined; the Lean claim there would read 0 ≤ 0 anyway. So the Lean theorem is the source claim plus a trivially true conjunct, and the two are equivalent.

review.notes: No findings. Lean experiments in /workspace/review/: (1) A computable Nat copy of `NG` gives the hand-computed values on P3 (1), C4 (2), C5 (3), K_{3,3} (3), K5 minus an edge (3 = n-2), the 5-vertex star (1) and P5 (2); on K4 it returns none (no non-edges). (2) Proved `NG P3 = 1` and `NG (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 4)) = 4`, the `Fintype.card` fallback. (3) Proved `(3 : ℝ) ≤ Ls (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 4))` using the spanning star, `spanningCoeEquivCoeOfSpanning` and `Iso.isTree_iff`. This confirms that `Ls` counts degree-1 vertices of spanning trees correctly, and that the tight complete-graph case NG - 1 = n - 1 ≤ Ls holds. The comparison is in ℝ, so there is no truncated subtraction. `Ls` = 0 only for disconnected graphs, which the connectivity hypothesis excludes. The category `research solved` matches the source's 'T' (proved by DeLaVina 1996 in the original list), so there is no status issue. The original cms.dt.uh.edu site is unreachable over HTTPS from the sandbox; all source text came from Wayback Machine snapshots.
